reason: The text demonstrates that Yahweh cares about both the Hebrew leaders and the people. While the narrative preserves young King Joash (the leader), it explicitly shows the people receiving substantial benefits: all the people of the land are described as rejoicing (וַיִּשְׂמַ֥ח כָּל־ עַם־ הָאָ֖רֶץ), the city becomes peaceful (שָׁקָ֑טָה), and the people actively participate in a covenant between Yahweh, the king, and themselves (לִהְי֥וֹת לְעָ֖ם לַֽיהוָ֑ה). The people are further empowered to collectively destroy idolatrous worship. The narrative presents no evidence of Yahweh lacking empathy for the people; rather, it shows the people benefiting from divine action alongside the preservation of legitimate leadership. The statement presents a false dichotomy by suggesting care for leaders must preclude empathy for the people, when the text indicates both groups benefit.
